Pile technologies are grouped into three families by method of construction: replacement piles (CFA pile, grabbed barrette, large-diameter bored piles), displacement piles (cast-in-place screw pile, precast concrete or steel tube driven/vibrated pile, precast steel screw pile, Franki pile), and micropiles made with a casing and a sacrificial bit. In the diagram they are completed by an “other” group: jet grouting, deep mixing and stone columns, which already lead towards ground improvement. (The complete system of deep foundations, including diaphragm walls and well and box foundations, is shown in section 1.2.) Tap a branch to jump to the relevant chapter. The Franki pile is a driven, “monolithic” concrete pile of high bearing capacity, made with a recovered casing. Most often approx. 1 m of dry concrete is placed in the bottom of a casing tube 46–52 cm in diameter, with 30 mm wall thickness and 13 m long (extendable), and rammed inside the tube with a 3 t drop hammer. Through friction the plug drags the tube down with it – the tube goes down without any soil or water getting into it.

One of the most frequently used piling technologies in Hungary: a pile that is quick to build and “efficient”. Its name abbreviates Continuous Flight Auger; in German-speaking countries it is known as the SOB pile, in France as the STARSOL pile. CFA is a replacement pile made with a continuous hollow auger; at the bottom of the auger there is a concreting outlet (with a closing plate).

During grouting, attention must be paid to the free outflow of the excess material – the cement grout returning to the surface. If it becomes blocked along the hole, the pressure builds up in the soil: hydraulic fracturing can occur, and in extreme cases the building or its surroundings may even be lifted by the excess cement.

The displacement drilling head works well in loose to medium-dense granular, intermediate and weakly cohesive (soft–firm) soil: it pushes aside and compacts the soil. It cannot penetrate a hard, very dense layer.

In rock, hard (stony) clay, strongly cemented soil and fill with large blocks driving can only be used to a limited extent – often even a thin such intercalation stops the pile. In loose and medium-dense sand driving (vibrating) works well, and the displacement even compacts the soil.

With a noise and vibration limit, CFA is the obvious choice: fast, monitored, 40–120 cm, at most 22–24 m. In loose to medium-dense granular and intermediate soil the screw pile is also good: no dynamic effect or noise, and hardly any spoil.

Large-diameter piles (above 80 cm) can only be made by replacement. The casing is safe even in unfavourable silty soil, and bentonite-supported drilling works in any soil: both are made 80–150 (350) cm in diameter, to a depth of at most approx. 100 m (in Hungary so far 30–40 m).

The drilling head of the screw pile pushes aside and compacts the soil while drilling: the shaft resistance increases, only a little spoil comes to the surface, and there is no dynamic effect or noise. In loose to medium-dense granular and intermediate soils it is a popular, economical and fast solution for moderately loaded industrial facilities (drilling head diameter 300–700 mm, maximum length 18 (20) m).

In cohesive soil, mainly above the groundwater, for piles that are not too long (approx. 8–10 m), the bore may remain stable for a short time even without support – but it must be concreted immediately after excavation. Slurry is an unnecessary cost here, and the caisson and the diaphragm wall are structures an order of magnitude larger.

Pile driving causes significant noise and vibration, so near structures it can only be used to a limited extent – next to vibration-sensitive neighbours it is the riskiest. CFA is chosen specifically where noise and vibration are restricted, the screw pile has no dynamic effect or noise, and the micropile is made with a small rig, without vibration.

Cutter Soil Mixing resembles diaphragm walling with a hydrofraise (cutter), but here only binder is introduced into the ground and the local soil is mixed. With CSM a continuous wall reinforced with steel members can be formed; the panels are approx. 50–60 cm wide and 10–15 m deep.
there is rock or very hard clay – then it can only be built with a hydrofraise

The slurry cycle in hydrofraise trenching: the soil-laden slurry (brown) taken from the trench is cleaned by the desander, and the cleaned and fresh slurry (greenish-yellow) returns to the trench from the tank – so the slurry level in the trench can be kept above the groundwater table throughout.

In Hungary the hydrofraise has so far been deployed in the construction of metro line 4 in Budapest: a diaphragm wall was built 40 m deep at Szent Gellért tér and 48.3 m deep at Fővám tér, right next to the Danube.

In rock and very hard clay a diaphragm wall can only be built with a hydrofraise (a reverse-circulation trench cutter with cutter wheels). It is very expensive, but it gives an accurate trench to great depth, in any soil and rock.
In rock and very hard clay only with a hydrofraise – very expensive.

In rock or very hard clay a diaphragm wall can only be built with a hydrofraise: the cutter wheels break up the material, which is pumped out together with the slurry and then separated outside. It is very expensive, but it gives an accurate trench to great depth, in any soil and rock. In Hungary it was used for the construction of metro line 4: diaphragm walls 48.3 m deep at Fővám tér and 40 m deep at Szent Gellért tér. Sheet piles cannot be driven into rock.
